sections.title: Interview with Michelle Ciulla Lipkin

sections.text: We are joined now by Michelle Ciulla Lipkin. Michelle, welcome to the Skeptics Guide.
Thanks for having me.

Now we we had to have you on the show because we noticed that you are the executive director of the National Association for Media Literacy Education. And media literacy is something that we do, so we thought it'd be fun to chat with someone who's basically, that there's significant overlap with what we do but not quite from the same perspective. Because we are, I think you know we started doing what we're doing with scientific literacy. But we sort of figured out late in the game that media literacy has to be a component of what we're doing. So why don't you give us a primer? What do you do, why is media literacy important, just tell us about your organization.

Great. Thanks again for having me on. I love talking about media literacy and it's a real pleasure to be on and talk to people that care about this as much as I do. So I am the executive director of namely and we are an organization that really acts as a convener and a resource and a thought leader in the media literacy space in the US. And we are the largest membership organization for media literacy education. And we've actually been in existence since 1997. And that shocks people. Because most of you have not been thinking about media literacy since 1997 but we certainly have been. And we were started by a group of academics that really started to look at media effects. And how we teach and how we read and write in all contexts. And so we really think about media literacy as the 21st century literacy, right? What do we need what do we need to be literate in today's world. And we really do need to be able to consume an author with all types of media attacks. And so our organization has been doing this work for quite some time, and really since 2016 it seems like everyone's starting to pay a lot of attention, to the work and to the importance of it. Which is both exciting and daunting for all of us.
So yeah, so you're kind of in the same boat we are in a way. So you started doing what you're doing or your organization, at least in the before time, you know, before social media.
When did we start, do we start in 96?
Yeah, 96.
Kinda like [inaudible] but that's okay. (Cara laughs)

And in the last 20-30 years the world has gone to hell. From a media literacy, scientific literacy perspective. And you know, so is that our fault? Or is it just we, or is it thank goodness we were at least we were doing this it would be so much worse.
Right. Teaspoon-ocean.
Yeah. Yeah it's interesting because I, you might not like this, I know you're skeptical but I am a very positive optimistic person. I can't help it. Even when I try not to be it comes out.
Me too. (Cara laughs)

And I actually think, I don't think the world is going to shit. I think we have a lot of issues and we have a lot of you know new systems, new communications, new ways in which we connect and communicate, that we don't quite understand yet. But I still am in that that belief system, that these tools that we have at our disposal are really empowering, and really exciting, and really creative. And I think we just gotta figure out how to how to make sure we're using them for good and not evil. So I want to feel optimistic. I know there's, I know there's a lot of crap out there, believe me. But I do don't, I don't think I could do the work that I do every day without thinking that there is a lot of potential out there in the media system for us to take advantage of.
So you're not burned out yet, that's sweet.

I'm not burned out yet and it's interesting because I've been doing, I've been at namely, this is my 10th year. And I have seen such change, and maybe that's, you know what, maybe that's why I'm optimistic. People used to not return my calls, you know? And it took a really long time to just explain why people needed to be thinking about this. And now the change in the brief amount of time. And really the shift came, you know in, you know there were there were a couple of shifts. Once, one obviously the advent of social media and the impact that that had. But then of course 2016 and and the election and what that did for people understanding social media, and algorithms, and data collection and all of that. And then the advent of, not the advent, but the throwing fake news into the cultural conversation. You know just people started to realize like wow, we have a lot of problems, how are we going to solve them? And then add the pandemic as I'm sure your phone has been ringing off the hook, like there are so many layers to this that have just risen to the top that have made this work so urgent. And for someone that's been doing it for a long time, the fact that I don't need to prove that it's urgent, and I can just get into the how. Like what do we need to do is so heartening to me and so exciting because it means that we can get something done. Am I being too optimistic for this? (laughter)
First of all skeptics are not cynics.
True, and I appreciate that.
Except Bob.
We're all optimists otherwise we would not still be we've been doing this for 26 years. I mean we would not still be doing this if we were not optimists.
That's adorable.

And I agree with you, I've had the same experience. I don't have to explain what we do. Like 30 years ago people had no idea what this was all about. They were like I don't get it, like what do you mean, do you investigate ghosts? I mean, what are you doing. And now it's like thank god you guys are doing what you're doing. You know because it's so much more obvious like yeah you talk about we want to give people critical thinking skills. Like oh please, do that, whatever it whatever it takes. Of course everyone thinks that about everybody else, you know?
Right.
No matter what side you're on, you think that the other side lacks critical thinking skills.
Absolutely.

But I'm sure it's the same with media literacy, I think every, you agree with that? Does it my sense is that everyone thinks media on the other side horrible, terrible, evil and only their media is legitimate. How do you combat that?
Well also everyone thinks that they're immune to it.
Yeah.

You know they're like, oh no media messages don't impact me. (Cara laughs) You know like oh no I'm not affected by the advertising I see on Instagram, like nothing, you know, like it's so interesting that every, it is a problem for everyone else but not me. I mean, I think what we try to do with media literacy you know, one of the issues that we've kind of come up against is that over the past few years, there's been a rise in conversation about misinformation, disinformation, fake news. And so that has kind of narrowed the focus a bit, when people think about media literacy they think about, you know asking the question, oh how do I know this is true and and kind of equate fact checking with media literacy education. And the truth is is that fact checking is very much a tool, in the toolbox but media literacy wants us to go much further and much deeper to critically think and you know effectively analyze all of the media we create and consume, right? So when I do hear the kind of like this side, that side, or you know when we try to kind of talk in binaries you know like true or false, I try to expand the conversation a bit. Because, there's not two sides, there's a million sides most of the time when it comes to the content that we are viewing. And most of the media messages out there are not, don't fall kind of completely in falsehoods and completely in truth, right? There's a lot of gray area that we need to understand. And so what we try to do is talk about, yeah no, obviously we want to identify disinformation but we also want to understand it, right? And so I think that, not that I'm saying that the people that are like, you know, this is how the you know, this side feels or that side feels, like I think that's an opening to a much deeper conversation that we should be having. Because I think that humans are nuanced and messages are nuanced and we need to be willing to dive in a little deeper.

Yeah so you have your own demarcation problem, right? Just like, and there's always a demarcation problem. Science and pseudoscience, skepticism and denial, fake news at real news. It all just sort of a mishmash in the middle. And but it's hard, it's hard to teach people nuance because they like the simple message, right? Don't you think?

And also that our systems, like social media isn't built for nuance you know. So we have systems in place that are are kind of built their structure is to polarize. You know there's not a lot of nuanced conversation happening on our feeds because that's not the language of these platforms. And so that makes it tricky also. It kind of drives that you know, either-or, my side-your side kind of conversation. And we do need to to be a little bit, not a little bit, we need to be a lot careful with that because, you know it's just the world isn't, real life is not that way. People are complicated. They have complicated thoughts and values and beliefs and we have to figure out a way to to not forget that given the fact that our like, like our main source of communication is kind of fighting us. And trying to really create these systems that are very binary and very true-false, wrong-right, it just, that isn't really how information works.
Right, but you got to upvote or downvote, right? You only got two options.
Yes, yes. Like or don't like, comment or don't, you know like, that's, it's hard, it's not built for nuance.
Do you have your, like short list of what is media literacy like, what are the, what are the core principles you want to educate the public about in terms of media literacy skills?

Yeah, so the way that we define media literacy is, it's the ability to access, analyze, evaluate, create an act using all forms of communication. So it's really important that we're not talking about just analyzing and and evaluating, right? We also are talking about that creation step and also talking about action. And it's important to note that that action was actually, is a relatively new addition to the definition because it is something that came with the advent of social media living in a participatory culture, looking at you know the way that we interact and engage as participants. So we need to also really understand what our role is and what is, kind of the parameters in which we navigate this, not only as consumers, we're no longer passive consumers, we're active participants in these media systems. So what does that mean and what is it, what does that mean as as far as my role and where I fit into the whole system. But we do have core principles, we do have six core principles that we talk about and I you know certainly don't wanna bore your listeners with them but essentially it's really framing it as you know an expanded definition of literacy. Talking about how it it's kind of built and reinforced with integrated practice, meaning that it's not something that you can just learn overnight, right? Just like foundational literacy, this is the, these are skills that need to be taught from the earliest ages on. And really looking about how media are part of our culture. And that people use their individual skills, and beliefs, and life experiences to construct their own meanings for media messages. And that's a really important one that, you know we have to be willing to understand our biases, the biases of those that create and construct the media. And really understand that you know, there's no way that every single, there's no way that two people are going to respond the exact same way to media messages. And we have to recognize that, something that I talk about a lot. I teach at Brooklyn College and we talk about that a lot, about how there's just no way I can see the world exactly how my students see it. And they can't see it the way I see it, so what makes us think that we could understand media messages the same. So yeah, so there's some core principles and guidelines that we use to frame media literacy. And there's other groups. We have 90 organizations within our umbrella, so there's a lot of really really good work being done. We have 7 000 members and you know, work being done all across the country that is really quite extraordinary. From a local, regional, community-based efforts but also national efforts. It's really been, it's just been a really incredible time for the media literacy space.

So you have the name you know, the word education right in your name and that is again also like our first approach, like how do we make people more you know, the world more logical. It's like well education is the first our first go-to tool. But do you think there are limits to what we can achieve with that? And do we need to? Like as you say do you know we need to talk about how to change the social media algorithms? Are the algorithms going to overwhelm education eventually if we don't pay attention to that as well?

Yeah well I would say that it has to be a multi-stakeholder solution, because it's certainly a multi-stakeholder problem. I think that what I hear more often than not. And I'm not sure if this is happening in your space but I actually hear a lot about you know regulating the social media companies, the transparencies around the algorithm. And I tend to hear like, to not hear education within the conversation. So we're kind of fighting to say, no, that we have to do all that. But we are not going to make change unless we are changing the way we educate our students, and educate this next generation on how they navigate this world. And also thinking about continuing education because adults are really struggling to navigate this world, because they never learned how to do it either. So I think that education, I think the challenge with education is just the time and effort and the lack of speed, right? It's very difficult to get into the education system and shift the way we do things. And do it in a way that is deliberate and effective, and strategic. And that's the long game. And I find that especially with the arguments that we have, or maybe not the arguments, the conversations we're having about miss and disinformation. We're looking for those short-term solutions. We want to stop it, we want to combat it we want to make it go away. And the problem is education is slow, right? Education takes time, education takes thought. And there's not a lot of people that have the patience for it, right? And so we have to, we have to play the long game and we have to you know kind of battle those folks that are like, okay I can just pass this policy right now and you know regulate the social media companies. Not that that's happening yet, but yes and, what are we doing in our education system? And like I said we have great work going on in the US. But in the education system itself, there's, you know, only one state that even requires a media literacy course. And you know, it's just not in any way a national priority and that is you know, it's atrocity that we're trying to solve. You know like this is, this is key to people succeeding in the world.
We have similar obstacles as well that we've experienced in skepticism, absolutely.

Yeah, what's more important to teach students than media literacy, right? I mean we live in a world where the the divide between those who can access useful information and those who can't, obviously it's a continuum, but that may be the number one determiner of your quality of life in a lot of ways, right? The wealthiest people in our society are dying due to their own media illiteracy or lack of critical thinking skills. I, you know, we tend to think of these things all together. So yeah, absolutely, and again like yeah, we want to teach critical thinking in schools, and scientific literacy. The problem, one problem that sort of we've run into, is that like critical thinking became a buzzword in education. Not sure that they're teaching what we would consider real critical thinking skills, you know what I mean? Just kind of paying at lip service and they're doing things that are sort of critical thinking but, so you know, my concern would be, yeah media literacy becomes a new sort of education buzzword ut is it really doing what we needed to do? That's been a, I agree, it's been a very hard space to crack, the education culture.

Yeah and I think yeah because, yeah and you just hit on it, because you can break into it, but what if it's not well done, right? So what if it's bad, what if it's bad media literacy practice? And you know, and that, that is tough. And so that's why we, I don't know where you guys lean in terms of like where your efforts like, where you focus your efforts, but for us it's teacher training. Like for us it's not as much there are so many resources out there, so much curriculum, so many lesson plans, it's amazing. But, if we're not training teachers, how to bring it into their classroom or not training teachers how to kind of integrate the media literacy skill building into English and science, and math, and all the other subjects, then we're not going to get anywhere. So to us it's like, what about the teacher training schools, how are we teaching people to teach this? Is really an important question we ask.

Yeah, absolutely. Yeah you know, we would love to do more of that. We've done seminars and of course you know we, our podcast, a lot of teachers listen to that, use it in their classroom, a lot of teachers use our book in their classroom. And so that, I agree, that is critical, that's something I would like to do more of actually.
We need our book in every classroom. (Jay laughs)

And of course you know, we're talking about us, meaning the five of us on this show. But there's also us this, the broader skeptical community, which is you know, very, it's a more of a loose multi-faceted sort of common purpose organization. It's not really organized from the top down. It's more bottom-up. So just a lot of people doing different things. But that, I agree, that educating educators is─
Yes.
─that's I think where a lot of the game is right there.

And that, and think about this environment right now, you know? The last thing educators need right now is is more stuff, right? And and they're so exhausted, and so beat down, they, it has been such a difficult time for them. You know, from the pandemic, to the book banning to you know you just hear about the you know the kind of experience teachers are having right now, and we have to do a not beyond media literacy and critical thinking we have to do a lot to reframe that profession and make sure it's something that people want to do and want to explore, because it's been a really tough time for teachers.

Yeah, I agree, I think education is going through its transition, it's a little slow and it's may be hard to see but you know, what's the role of education in a world but you can get access to any information you want at your fingertips you know on social media. You know, I think it's what, I guess again, it gets back to, they need to teach people how to access and evaluate information. Because it's all there, they don't, we don't need the educational system to provide information, it's all there. We just need them to teach kids how to think, how to be critical thinkers, how to access information, how to be media literate, right?

Yeah I mean, I think that that you know, that's a really good point and I think that if you really think about it, what we need is a revolution in education, right? Like if we really think about it, we need to to change you know how we think about, what, like when we think about the kind of that phrase "what does it mean to be college and career ready", you know? How are you not teaching them these skills? Like because isn't that you know, it doesn't quite matter what you do after you graduate high school or college, you're gonna need these skills, right? They're, you know, going to be forever valuable and needed. So it's, that's one of the reasons that we are we have a conference every year and our conference is coming up. We're doing it virtually again July 15th to 17th and it's called. The theme is Level Up: Building a Media Literate World. And really what we're trying to do is bring together that conversation which is, okay great, we're doing good work, but how do we level up, how do we take it to the next level? How do we scale? How do we make this the national priority that it needs to be? One thing I would love to share just with everyone listening is that we are a free membership organization. So if you're interested in media literacy and you want to join you know it is totally free, it's that join button on our namle.net web home page. And besides our conference we also host US media literacy week which is October 24th to 28th and it's a great opportunity to like do stuff in your community around media literacy and also attend you know virtual or community based events. So I just wanted to let people know if they're interested in learning more and getting involved, there are ways to do that.

Great, yeah, that's n-a-m-l-e.net and you have a lot of, you have a resource page on your website, I've been looking through a lot of good articles on there. A parent's guide to media literacy and fighting misinformation about coronavirus. So a lot of good resources there for our audience if they're interested in checking it out. Well Michelle thank you so much for joining us on the show. It's always good to talk with people who are sort of intersecting the skeptical movement but not, you know, not 100% overlap and it's, it sounds like you're facing a lot of the same things we are.
Absolutely, I really appreciate chatting with you and just also learning a little bit about what you are all doing.
Great, thanks again for coming. Take care.
Thank you.
Thank you very much.

And item #3: A reexamination of data demonstrates that as many as 20% of exoplanets previously validated through the transmit method are instead small stars.

Okay, Jay.
